name: Add-ins
description:
Adversaries may abuse Microsoft Office add-ins to obtain persistence on a compromised system. Office add-ins can be used to add functionality to Office programs. (Citation: Microsoft Office Add-ins) There are different types of add-ins that can be used by the various Office products; including Word/Excel add-in Libraries (WLL/XLL), VBA add-ins, Office Component Object Model (COM) add-ins, automation add-ins, VBA Editor (VBE), Visual Studio Tools for Office (VSTO) add-ins, and Outlook add-ins. (Citation: MRWLabs Office Persistence Add-ins)(Citation: FireEye Mail CDS 2018)

Add-ins can be used to obtain persistence because they can be set to execute code when an Office application starts.

references.description: Caban, D. and Hirani, M. (2018, October 3). You’ve Got Mail! Enterprise Email Compromise. Retrieved November 17, 2024.
Knowles, W. (2017, April 21). Add-In Opportunities for Office Persistence. Retrieved November 17, 2024.
Microsoft. (n.d.). Add or remove add-ins. Retrieved July 3, 2017.
Shukrun, S. (2019, June 2). Office Templates and GlobalDotName - A Stealthy Office Persistence Technique. Retrieved August 26, 2019.

telemetry.name: Application Log Content
telemetry.description: Application-emitted audit or operational event content.
telemetry.collection_focus: Select the application event family required by the detection and document its native schema before normalization.

providers.name: Application audit logs
providers.scope: First-party service events and request/result fields; schema is application-specific.

providers.name: OpenTelemetry-compatible log pipelines
providers.scope: Transport and normalization of emitted records; do not create missing audit instrumentation.

configuration: Enable the application audit category or instrument the owned lab application at the authorization/action boundary.
Define a schema with timestamp, service, actor, object, action, result and correlation ID. Export structured records through an authenticated collector.
Redact secrets and personal content, separate audit from debug logs, set retention and verify delivery during rotation/restart.
telemetry.example_note: Project-normalized synthetic JSON, not a native provider log, captured event, attack verdict or validated detection. A parser/adapter is required for a real SIEM. Example names, IPs and values are fictional.
telemetry.limitations: Debug output is not necessarily a durable audit trail. Application developers must emit the relevant event; installing a log pipeline does not make an absent event exist.
telemetry.anomaly_design: Per application, client and route: request rate, rare actions, failure ratios and unusual state transitions. Version changes, retries, health probes and seasonal load need separate baselines.

telemetry.name: Command Execution
telemetry.description: Execution of a command and its interpreter or parent context.
telemetry.collection_focus: Collect process command lines and relevant shell/interpreter audit; shell history alone is neither complete nor tamper-resistant.

providers.name: PowerShell Script Block Logging
providers.scope: Script content via event 4104 when configured; channel depends on PowerShell edition.

providers.name: Sysmon process events
providers.scope: Interpreter launch and parent context, not full script content.

providers.name: Linux Audit
providers.scope: execve-family execution context; shell built-ins need additional instrumentation.

configuration: Enable Script Block Logging through the policy/configuration for the installed edition. Forward Microsoft-Windows-PowerShell/Operational for Windows PowerShell, or PowerShellCore/Operational for PowerShell 7.
Retain script-block ID and fragment ordering alongside process creation. Protect access to collected script text; secrets may be included.
On Linux, use narrowly scoped Audit execution rules for the lab account and supported architectures, and retain joined SYSCALL/EXECVE/PATH records.
telemetry.example_note: Project-normalized synthetic JSON, not a native provider log, captured event, attack verdict or validated detection. A parser/adapter is required for a real SIEM. Example names, IPs and values are fictional.
telemetry.limitations: Script content and process command lines are different signals. Logging may be partial, fragmented, filtered or disabled; never assume a command line reveals everything executed.
telemetry.anomaly_design: Per host role and principal: rare interpreters, command argument patterns and parent-child sequences. Normalize scripts carefully; obfuscation, administrative automation and missing command lines change visibility.

telemetry.name: File Creation
telemetry.description: Creation or overwrite of a file at an observed path.
telemetry.collection_focus: Scope Sysmon FileCreate (11) to the lab directory; retain the process and file path. Differentiate creation/overwrite if the sensor can.

Forward Microsoft-Windows-Sysmon/Operational to the lab collector. Preserve event ID, timestamp, computer, process identifiers and the original event.
For Linux or macOS, select the equivalent sensor separately and test its emitted fields; a Windows event ID does not transfer across platforms.

strategies.name: Detect Persistence via Malicious Office Add-ins

analytics.name: Analytic 0137
analytics.guidance: An adversary writes or drops a malicious Office Add-in (e.g., WLL, XLL, COM) to a trusted directory or modifies registry keys to load malicious add-ins on Office application launch. Upon user opening Word or Excel, the add-in is automatically loaded, triggering execution of the payload, often spawning scripting engines or anomalous child processes.

tuning.description: Malicious add-ins may have varying extensions (.wll, .xll, .dll, .vsto)
Office trusted add-in paths may differ across enterprise configurations
Registry keys used to load add-ins may be version- and app-specific
Office processes spawning mshta.exe, powershell.exe, or rundll32.exe are abnormal
Add-in loading may occur only during Office launch windows

analytics.name: Analytic 0138
analytics.guidance: Malicious Office add-ins loaded via VSTO, COM, or VBA auto-load paths. Upon launch of Word/Excel/Outlook, the add-in executes code without user action. Add-in resides in trusted directory or registered via Office COM/VBE subsystem. Behavior includes unsigned add-in execution, anomalous load context, or add-in spawning interpreter process.

tuning.description: Admins may allow or block unsigned add-ins depending on GPO configuration
Different Office versions store trusted paths and add-in configs in version-specific locations
Some add-ins only load on specific actions (new document, open file, etc.)

mitigations.name: Behavior Prevention on Endpoint
mitigations.description: On Windows 10, enable Attack Surface Reduction (ASR) rules to prevent Office applications from creating child processes and from writing potentially malicious executable content to disk. (Citation: win10_asr)

references.description: Microsoft. (2021, July 2). Use attack surface reduction rules to prevent malware infection. Retrieved June 24, 2021.

candidates.name: Persistent Code Execution Via Excel VBA Add-in File (XLAM)
candidates.description:
Creates an Excel VBA Add-in file (XLAM) which runs automatically when Excel is started
The sample XLAM provided launches the notepad as a proof-of-concept for persistent execution from Office.

dependencies.description: XLAM file must exist on disk at specified location

candidates.name: Code Executed Via Excel Add-in File (XLL)
candidates.description:
Loads an XLL file using the excel add-ins library.
This causes excel to launch Notepad.exe as a child process. This atomic test does not include persistent code execution as you would typically see when this is implemented in malware.

dependencies.description: XLL files must exist on disk at specified location

candidates.name: Persistent Code Execution Via Word Add-in File (WLL)
candidates.description:
Creates a Word Add-in file (WLL) which runs automatically when Word is started
The sample WLL provided launches the notepad as a proof-of-concept for persistent execution from Office.
Successfully tested on 32-bit Office 2016. Not successful from microsoft 365 version of Office.

dependencies.description: WLL files must exist on disk at specified location

candidates.name: Persistent Code Execution Via Excel Add-in File (XLL)
candidates.description:
Creates an Excel Add-in file (XLL) and sets a registry key to make it run automatically when Excel is started
The sample XLL provided launches the notepad as a proof-of-concept for persistent execution from Office.

dependencies.description: XLL files must exist on disk at specified location

candidates.name: Persistent Code Execution Via PowerPoint VBA Add-in File (PPAM)
candidates.description:
Creates a PowerPoint VBA Add-in file (PPAM) which runs automatically when PowerPoint is started
The sample PPA provided launches the notepad as a proof-of-concept for persistent execution from Office.

dependencies.description: PPAM file must exist on disk at specified location
